Typical values depend on the dataset size and the desired ROI.
*   **Depth Order:** When cutting planes are active, standard depth buffering may fail if the entry/exit points are not correctly tracked.
*   **Arbitrary Positions:** Cropping planes can be placed at non-integer coordinates.
*   **Invalid Regions:** If $x_{min} > x_{max}$, the region is empty.
*   **Boundary Artifacts:** At the cropping boundaries, discontinuities may occur.
Clipping geometry makes parts of the volume transparent.
*   **Time Complexity:** $O(N)$, where $N$ is the number of voxels in the cropped region.
Cropping reduces the effective $N$ by excluding voxels outside the ROI, thus improving performance proportionally to the volume of the ROI relative to the full volume.
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(1)$ additional memory for storing the six plane coordinates.
*   **Strengths:** Simple to implement; effective for focusing on specific features; reduces computational load; axis-aligned nature allows for efficient spatial partitioning and culling.

*   **When to use:** When the user needs to inspect internal structures by removing outer layers; when performance is critical and the ROI is small; when the ROI is naturally axis-aligned (e.g., a specific organ in a medical scan aligned with the scanner axes).

*   **When not to use:** When the ROI is oriented at an arbitrary angle; when the user needs to see the relationship between the cropped region and the rest of the volume in a single view without deformation (use [Focus+Context Visualization via Deformation](3001-focus-context-visualization-via-deformation.md) instead).
Cropping originated as a fundamental interaction technique in volume visualization to allow users to "see inside" volumetric datasets.
